EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon on the 23rd a cold front crossed the Northeast. Later that evening a strong, secondary cold front crossed the region with heavy snow showers and bitterly cold temperatures. Widespread temperatures below zero and gusty winds were observed by the morning of the 24th. Key messages: dangerous wind chills, business closures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: During the early morning on the 24th temperatures plunged below zero. Strong cold air advection allowed mechanical mixing to occur through the night. Sustained winds of 15 to 20 mph, and frequent gusts even higher, led to wind chills of 25 to 40 below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An expansive winter storm gripped much of the country beginning on the 24th. An anomalously cold air mass was in place ahead of the storm, which tracked through the southern Plains and across the Southeast. A significant cold air dam remained in place east of the Appalachian Mountains and helped to force secondary cyclogenesis south of New England on the 25th. Strong warm air advection in the mid levels forced an intense band of snow that lifted north through New England, reaching New Hampshire and western Maine during the afternoon. Snow quickly became moderate to heavy after onset. Snowfall rates were at times one inch or more per hour as the band lifted northward. In its wake lower level forcing continued the moderate to heavy snow near the Massachusetts border through the overnight into the morning of the 26th. This resulted in the highest snowfall totals across southeast New Hampshire and southwestern Maine. The upper level trough swung through the region on the 26th with light snow for much of the day, ending as one final burst of moderate snow in the evening. Key message: heavy snow, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow overspread southeast New Hampshire by midday on the 25th. Within an hour or two snow was moderate to heavy at times as an intense band of lift moved into the region. Snowfall rates were one to two inches per hour during the heavy snow. Snow continued overnight into the 26th, with occasional breaks or lighter snowfall before the storm center moved into the Atlantic. Snowfall totals ranged from 14 to 18 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, New Hampshire remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 41% of New Hampshire were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. New Hampshire exhibited highly variable precipitation patterns in March 2026. While the state continued to observe below-normal accumulations and persistent hydrologic strain, central sections along the Merrimack valley and White Mountains experienced modest precipitation surpluses. The onset of seasonal thaw provided minor, superficial relief to shallow soil layers, but slow-responding deep groundwater tables remained severely depleted, with many monitoring locations lingering near or below the 25th percentile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Belknap County averaged 3.21 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.25 inches below normal, extending the deficits since June up to 8 inches. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).

As of late March, 41% of New Hampshire were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. New Hampshire exhibited highly variable precipitation patterns in March 2026. While the state continued to observe below-normal accumulations and persistent hydrologic strain, central sections along the Merrimack valley and White Mountains experienced modest precipitation surpluses. The onset of seasonal thaw provided minor, superficial relief to shallow soil layers, but slow-responding deep groundwater tables remained severely depleted, with many monitoring locations lingering near or below the 25th percentile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coos County averaged 2.68 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.54 inches below normal, marking the 3rd driest June through March stretch on record with deficits over 8 inches. The USDM on March 31st had 42% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 58% in Moderate Drought (D1).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm storm brought mountain snow-melt, heavy rain and gusty winds as a potent low pressure system pushed across the area March 16-17th.  This caused some minor ice jams, but no ice left its banks during this event.  Rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches fell over the 36 hour period leading to rapid stream and river rises across the state.  A few rivers reached minor flood stage, with most other rivers remaining just below flood stage or in action stage.  Long term drought helped mitigate flood conditions as base flow river levels where very low.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Saco River at Conway reached minor flood conditions on the morning of March 17. Numerous campgrounds flooded. The river reached 9.23 ft, exceeding the 7 ft flood stage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure began to develop over the Southeast on the morning of the 22nd. By the evening it had moved to a position off the Carolinas and was deepening rapidly. Between 7 pm on the 22nd and 7 am on the 23rd, central pressure in the storm dropped from 991 mb to 966 mb. The intense low pressure combined with high pressure around 1045 mb building into Quebec to produce a strong pressure gradient across the region. The result was strong wind gusts through much of the day on the 23rd. While the heaviest snowfall remained largely over southern New England, the edge of the heavy snow did move into southern New Hampshire. The combination of the two produced blizzard conditions and near-zero visibility at times. While winds continued to gust into the evening, snowfall tapered off in the late afternoon hours on the 23rd. Key Messages: blizzard conditions, heavy snow, strong wind gusts, dangerous travel, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow managed to lift into parts of southern New Hampshire. The heaviest snowfall was on the morning of the 23rd into the early afternoon before tapering off. Though it was not frequent, Manchester-Boston Regional Airport did observed blizzard conditions intermittently into the early afternoon. Snowfall totals ranged from 5 to 9 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In February 2026, New Hampshire���s drought conditions remained steady in their classification while experiencing ongoing hydrologic strain. By the end of the month, the state���s drought extent held firm with 41% categorized as Severe Drought (D2), 37% as Moderate Drought (D1), and 22% as Abnormally Dry (D0). Although seasonal snowpack remained near normal across much of the state, particularly on the slopes of the White Mountains, the water content was relatively low, and the snowpack peaked in late February, nearly three weeks earlier than usual. Deep soil frost depths between 6 and 20 inches created a cap that blocked melting snow and rain from recharging deep aquifers. Consequently, the majority of groundwater monitoring levels remained at or below the 25th percentile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Belknap County averaged 1.22 inches of precipitation in February, approximately 1.63 inches below normal, marking the 10th driest February. The USDM on February 24th had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the start of 2026, drought conditions were widespread across Central and Northern New Hampshire. Drought conditions as Percent Area of the state: D3 - 0%, D2 - 41%, D1 - 36%. January brought little relief to New Hampshire's drought conditions in these areas, as winter set in and frozen ground effectively halted any potential for significant groundwater recharge. January precipitation remained below to well below normal with most areas around 75% of normal range. Snowfall remained below normal outside of the White Mountains, snow water equivalent remained below normal for all areas except the immediate coast. Streamflow and ground water remained well below normal on all basins. Dry well reports in January began to slacken off compared to previous months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: January can be summarized by a frozen cap effect as well below normal temperatures and significant frost depths prevented any meaningful sub-surface water recharge.  In addition, precipitation remained below normal for the entire region for the month.  This led to a lower than normal snowpack for all areas except the north slopes of the White Mountains for the month.  Overall, conditions in January didn't improve the drought and drought remained in a steady state at the end of the month.
